stem: A 7-year-old boy has a soft 2-cm lump in the midline of the neck just below the hyoid bone. It rises when he sticks out his tongue. Ultrasound shows a normal thyroid gland in its usual position, and the lump became tender after a recent sore throat.
oneliner: 7M + midline neck lump below hyoid + rises with tongue protrusion + normal thyroid on ultrasound + tender after sore throat → which embryonic origin?
ask: The tract of this cyst most likely developed from which embryonic tissue?

options.A: Endoderm of the third pharyngeal pouch
options.C: Ectoderm of the second pharyngeal cleft
options.D: Endoderm of the fourth pharyngeal pouch
options.E: Neural crest cells of the pharyngeal arches

whyNot.A: Third-pouch endoderm gives the **thymus and inferior parathyroids**, not a **midline** tract that moves with the **tongue**
whyNot.C: Second-cleft remnants give a **lateral** neck cyst along the sternocleidomastoid; this lump is **midline**
whyNot.D: Fourth-pouch endoderm gives the **superior parathyroids**; it has no link to **tongue movement** or a midline tract
whyNot.E: Neural crest forms arch **cartilage and connective tissue**; a midline cyst that **rises with the tongue** is a duct remnant

answer: Endoderm at the foramen cecum (thyroglossal duct remnant)
why: A **midline** cyst below the hyoid that **rises with tongue protrusion** is a **thyroglossal duct cyst**. The thyroid begins as an **endodermal** outgrowth at the **foramen cecum** and descends to the neck; a duct that fails to involute leaves a cyst along the tract. The **normal thyroid on ultrasound** shows the gland itself descended.

idea.rule: The thyroid arises from endoderm at the foramen cecum; its descent tract can leave a midline cyst.
also: The tract runs from the foramen cecum down to the thyroid isthmus
Thyroid tissue that fails to descend stays as a lingual thyroid
Thyroglossal cysts move up with swallowing and tongue protrusion
Lateral neck cysts come instead from the second pharyngeal cleft

stem: In an embryo experiment, differentiation of the endoderm lining the lung bud is blocked, while the surrounding mesenchyme develops normally.
oneliner: Embryo experiment + lung bud endoderm differentiation blocked + surrounding mesenchyme normal → which structure fails?
ask: Development of which structure is most likely to fail?

options.C: Capillary network of the alveolar walls
options.D: Connective tissue of the visceral pleura

whyNot.A: Tracheal cartilage comes from the **surrounding mesenchyme**, which is **normal** in this embryo
whyNot.B: Bronchial smooth muscle comes from **mesenchyme**, not endoderm, and is normal here
whyNot.C: Capillaries come from **mesodermal** vascular tissue, which develops normally here
whyNot.D: Visceral pleura connective tissue comes from **mesoderm**, which is normal here

why: The **endoderm** of the lung bud forms the **epithelium** of the airways and alveoli, including the **type II pneumocytes** that secrete **surfactant**. Cartilage, smooth muscle, vessels and visceral pleura come from **splanchnic mesoderm**, which is intact.

idea.rule: Lung epithelium comes from endoderm; the cartilage, muscle, vessels and pleura around it come from mesoderm.
also: The laryngotracheal diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut endoderm
Type I and type II pneumocytes are both endodermal
Visceral pleura comes from splanchnic mesoderm; parietal pleura from somatic mesoderm
Goblet and club cells are also endodermal

stem: A newborn boy has respiratory distress and a sunken abdomen at birth. Chest x-ray shows loops of bowel in the left chest with the heart pushed to the right. At surgery the defect is in the posterolateral left diaphragm; the central tendon and the anterior muscular rim are intact.
oneliner: Newborn boy + respiratory distress + scaphoid abdomen + bowel in left chest + posterolateral left diaphragm defect + intact central tendon → which embryonic structure?
ask: Maldevelopment of which embryonic structure most likely caused this defect?

whyNot.A: The septum transversum forms the **central tendon**, which is **intact** here
whyNot.B: The esophageal mesentery forms the **crura** around the midline openings, not the **posterolateral** diaphragm
whyNot.D: Body wall muscle forms the **peripheral muscular rim**, and the anterior rim is **intact**
whyNot.E: The pleuropericardial folds separate the pericardial and pleural cavities; they do not close the **posterolateral** diaphragm

why: A **posterolateral left** defect with **bowel in the chest** and a **scaphoid abdomen** is a **Bochdalek hernia**. The **pleuroperitoneal membranes** close the posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canals, and the **left** canal closes later than the right, so failure is commonest on the left. Compression of the developing lung causes **pulmonary hypoplasia**, the main cause of death.

idea.rule: Diaphragm = septum transversum (central tendon) + pleuroperitoneal membranes (posterolateral) + body wall muscle (rim) + esophageal mesentery (crura).
also: Pleuroperitoneal membrane failure gives a left posterolateral Bochdalek hernia
The septum transversum forms the central tendon and carries the C3-C5 phrenic supply down
A Morgagni hernia is anterior, behind the sternum, and less common
Herniated bowel compresses the lung and causes pulmonary hypoplasia

stem: A 1-hour-old girl born at 28 weeks has grunting, nasal flaring and chest retractions. Chest x-ray shows fine ground-glass opacities, and a lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio in amniotic fluid taken before delivery was below 2.
oneliner: 1-hour-old girl born at 28 weeks + grunting and retractions + ground-glass lungs + L/S ratio below 2 → at what gestational age is surfactant mature?
ask: At about what gestational age does surfactant production normally become adequate?

whyNot.A: At this age the lung is still in the **pseudoglandular** stage with no alveoli or type II cells
whyNot.B: Type II cells only **begin** making surfactant around 20 weeks; the amount is far too low
whyNot.C: Production is rising but still too low, as her illness at **28 weeks** shows
whyNot.E: Surfactant is adequate well before term, since infants born at 36-37 weeks breathe normally

answer: About 35 weeks (L/S ratio of 2 or more)
why: Type II pneumocytes **begin** making surfactant around **20 weeks**, but mature amounts appear only at about **35 weeks**, when the **lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio reaches 2** or more. A **28-week** infant with a **low ratio** therefore develops **neonatal respiratory distress syndrome**.

idea.rule: Surfactant becomes adequate around 35 weeks, when the L/S ratio reaches 2 or more.
also: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents collapse
Maternal corticosteroids speed fetal lung maturation
Phosphatidylglycerol in amniotic fluid also signals lung maturity
